items.stem: Explain whether you agree that economic motives were the most important reason why European empires expanded in the 19th century. Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.answer: Agree: Industrial economies needed raw materials (rubber, cotton, palm oil, minerals) and markets. Investors and companies such as the British South Africa Company drove expansion. Disagree: Rivalry and prestige between powers (e.g. Germany’s late entry) caused a rush for land. Strategic aims, such as protecting the route to India via Suez, mattered. Religious and racial ideas (civilising mission) justified expansion. Technology made it possible. Judgement: Economic motives were central, but rivalry turned them into a rapid Scramble, and technology made it possible.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1 mark): one simple reason. Level 2 (2-3 marks): one explained reason for AND one against, with accurate detail.

items.stem: Study Source B, Jawaharlal Nehru’s speech to India’s Constituent Assembly, 14-15 August 1947. “At the stroke of the midnight hour, when the world sleeps, India will awake to life and freedom.” (a) Suggest the purpose of Source B. Explain your answer. (b) Explain one reason why Source B may be reliable and one reason why it may not be reliable.
items.answer: (a) To celebrate independence and inspire Indians with hope and unity at a difficult moment. (b) May be reliable: it is the actual speech made by India’s first Prime Minister at the moment of independence. May not be reliable: it is a celebratory speech, so it does not mention the violence of partition happening at the same time.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2] (b) 2 marks for each explained reason based on provenance (author, date, purpose) [4]

items.stem: Put these events in chronological order, starting with the earliest. A: Algeria won independence from France after an eight-year war. B: French forces were defeated at Dien Bien Phu in Vietnam. C: Zimbabwe became independent. D: Seventeen African countries gained independence, the “Year of Africa”.
items.markingKey: Correct order B, D, A, C (B 1954; D 1960; A 1962; C 1980). 2 marks all correct; 1 mark if one adjacent pair is reversed. [2]

items.stem: Explain two economic legacies of colonialism for newly independent countries.
items.answer: Economies depended on exporting one or two raw materials (e.g. copper, cocoa) with unstable prices; infrastructure linked mines to ports rather than connecting regions; few industries; debt and foreign ownership (neo-colonialism).
items.markingKey: 2 marks each explained legacy [4]

items.stem: Study Source B, a speech by British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan to the South African parliament, Cape Town, February 1960. “The wind of change is blowing through this continent, and whether we like it or not, this growth of national consciousness is a political fact.” Suggest the purpose of Source B. Explain your answer.
items.answer: To signal to South Africa and to British settlers that Britain would not resist African independence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark purpose; 1 mark link to author/audience/date [2]

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “the rapid division and colonisation of most of Africa by European powers between about 1880 and 1914”.
items.answer: Scramble for Africa

items.stem: A student writes: “By 1914 every country in Africa was ruled by a European power.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Ethiopia and Liberia remained independent.

items.stem: Explain how religious and racial ideas were used to justify empire.
items.answer: Missionaries wanted to spread Christianity; ideas of a “civilising mission” and social Darwinism claimed Europeans were superior and had a duty to rule – ideas now rejected as racist.
items.markingKey: 1 mark religion; 1 mark racial ideas; 1 mark evaluation [3]

items.stem: Approximate share of the land area of Africa controlled by different powers in 1914 (%): Britain 30, France 35, Germany 8, Belgium 8, Italy 7, Portugal 7, Spain 1, Independent 4. (a) Calculate the percentage controlled by European powers. (b) Calculate how many times larger the British share was than the German share.

Read Source C carefully. “Take up the White Man’s burden— / Send forth the best ye breed— / Go bind your sons to exile / To serve your captives’ need.” (The opening lines of Rudyard Kipling’s poem “The White Man’s Burden”, 1899.) Use your own knowledge to describe one aspect of attitudes that were used to justify empire that Source C does not show.
items.answer: The economic motives for empire or the resistance of colonised peoples.

items.stem: Source A is taken from a modern historian writing in 2015 about the Scramble for Africa. It says: “Between 1880 and 1914 European powers claimed almost the entire continent. Machine guns, steamships and quinine made conquest possible, while rivalry between the powers made it urgent.” Use it to answer the questions. (a) Is Source A a primary or a secondary source? Give a reason for your answer. (b) What can you infer from Source A about how and why Africa was colonised so quickly?
items.answer: (a) Secondary source: it was produced later by someone who was not there, using other evidence. (b) Technology made conquest possible and rivalry made it happen quickly.

items.stem: Name the term that matches this definition: “a system in which colonial officials governed a territory themselves, replacing local rulers”.
items.answer: Direct rule
items.markingKey: Direct rule: a system in which colonial officials governed a territory themselves, replacing local rulers. [1]

items.stem: Explain why armed resistance to colonial rule usually failed.
items.answer: European armies had machine guns and modern rifles; they used divide-and-rule and local allies; harsh reprisals and famine (e.g. after Maji Maji) crushed rebellions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason up to [3]

items.stem: Study Source C, an interview with an elderly Kenyan woman recorded by a historian in 1970 (adapted). “When the settlers came, our family’s best land became a coffee farm. My father had to work there to pay the hut tax, and we children were sent to the mission school to learn English.” What can you infer from Source C about the effects of colonial rule on Kenyan families?
items.answer: Colonial rule took African land for settler farms, forced men into wage labour through taxes and changed education.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “swaraj”?
options: The division of British India in 1947 into two independent states, India and Pakistan.
The campaign to buy Indian-made goods and boycott British imports.
Gandhi’s method of non-violent resistance, meaning “truth-force”.
items.answer: Self-rule or independence for India.
items.markingKey: Swaraj: self-rule or independence for India. [1]

items.stem: Explain why Gandhi’s methods of non-violent protest were effective.
items.answer: Mass, peaceful protests (boycotts, Salt March) involved millions of ordinary Indians, gained worldwide publicity and made British repression look unjust; arrests filled the jails and made India harder and costlier to govern.
items.markingKey: 1 mark mass support; 1 mark publicity/moral pressure; 1 mark cost to Britain [3]
